ai.definition: Civilisation-Scale Fusion Reactors are large-scale nuclear fusion devices designed to produce significant amounts of clean, sustainable energy on a scale required to meet the needs of an entire civilization.
ai.howItWorks: These reactors use advanced materials and quantum technologies to stabilize and control plasma states in fusion reactions. The process involves heating hydrogen isotopes (typically deuterium and tritium) to extremely high temperatures, creating plasma that fuses into helium, releasing energy in the form of heat and light.
ai.problemSolved: Addressing the global need for clean, abundant energy while reducing greenhouse gas emissions and reliance on fossil fuels.
ai.manufacturing: Requires advanced manufacturing techniques including vacuum baking, precise material handling, and complex assembly processes. The materials used must be able to withstand extreme temperatures and radiation levels.
ai.buildProcess: Involves multiple stages: initial design, component fabrication, reactor assembly, testing, and commissioning. Each stage requires rigorous quality control and safety protocols due to the high energy density of fusion reactions.
ai.costDrivers: High initial capital investment, advanced materials, specialized labor, and extensive R&D costs. Long-term operational costs are lower due to minimal fuel requirements and low maintenance needs.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is in the early stages of commercialization with ongoing research and development efforts aiming for practical deployment within the next few decades.
ai.regulation: Subject to stringent safety, environmental, and operational regulations. International cooperation is likely due to the global nature of the challenges and benefits involved.
ai.risks: Technical risks include achieving sustained fusion reactions, managing high-energy plasma states, and ensuring reactor safety. Economic risks involve high initial costs and potential market resistance to new technology.
ai.profitability: Potential for significant long-term profitability through reduced energy costs and increased sales of clean energy, but with high upfront investment and operational challenges.
ai.futureDevelopment: Ongoing research focuses on improving plasma confinement, developing more efficient materials, and reducing the overall cost of fusion reactors. Advances in quantum technologies may also play a role in future developments.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds to thousands of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and high-temperature processes.

glossary.def: A state of matter consisting of ions and free electrons, often described as a fourth state of matter after solid, liquid, and gas.
A nuclear reaction where light nuclei combine to form heavier nuclei, releasing energy in the process.
A heavy isotope of hydrogen with one proton and one neutron, used as a fuel in fusion reactors.
A radioactive isotope of hydrogen with one proton and two neutrons, used as a fuel in fusion reactors.

subsystems.name: Burning plasma core
subsystems.role: a self-heating deuterium–tritium plasma, held by magnets and kept stable for hours at a time.

subsystems.name: Breeding blanket
subsystems.role: absorbs the fusion neutrons and turns lithium into fresh tritium fuel.
parts: lithium ceramic pebbles or liquid lithium–lead

subsystems.name: Shield and vacuum vessel
subsystems.role: holds the vacuum, stops neutrons and protects the magnets.

subsystems.name: Exhaust and divertor
subsystems.role: strips heat and helium 'ash' from the plasma edge.

subsystems.name: Fuel plant
subsystems.role: extracts, purifies, stores and reinjects tritium — the part that makes the plant self-sustaining.

subsystems.name: Power conversion
subsystems.role: turns blanket heat into grid electricity.

subsystems.name: Remote maintenance and hot cell
subsystems.role: replaces activated components that no human can touch.

buildSteps.title: Design for replacement, not permanence
buildSteps.detail: The parts closest to the plasma become radioactive and wear out. The machine is split into sectors that remote robots can unbolt, lift out and rebuild, because a power plant that cannot be serviced cannot run.

buildSteps.title: Wind the magnets on industrial lines
buildSteps.detail: Kilometres of high-temperature superconducting tape are wound into coils that must survive huge electromagnetic forces, then tested cold before shipping as finished modules.

buildSteps.title: Build the fuel plant alongside the tokamak
buildSteps.detail: Tritium processing, isotope separation and storage are not add-ons: they are sized so the blanket breeds slightly more fuel than the plasma burns.

buildSteps.title: Raise the building and balance of plant
buildSteps.detail: A thick concrete bioshield, cranes rated for activated loads, a turbine hall, cooling water and a grid connection are built around the machine.

buildSteps.title: Assemble and align
buildSteps.detail: Sectors are welded and bolted in place to millimetre tolerance, magnets are fitted, and the whole assembly is checked again after the first thermal cycle.

buildSteps.title: Commission with hydrogen, then deuterium
buildSteps.detail: Early operation uses non-radioactive fuels to prove control, disruption handling and remote maintenance before any tritium is introduced.

buildSteps.title: Run deuterium–tritium campaigns
buildSteps.detail: The plant must hold a burning plasma for long pulses, extract bred tritium and demonstrate that components survive the neutron flux.

buildSteps.title: Close the fuel cycle
buildSteps.detail: Breeding as much tritium as is burned — not energy gain alone — decides whether the design can be repeated.

buildSteps.title: Duplicate
buildSteps.detail: Civilisation scale means factory throughput of superconducting tape, lithium-6 and remote-handling hardware, not one impressive machine.

prerequisites.why: a burning plasma that heats itself is essential; no tokamak has yet released more energy than it absorbed.
tritium barely exists in nature, so each plant must manufacture its own fuel from lithium.
structural and first-wall materials must survive years of neutron bombardment, not the weeks currently tested.
stronger magnets shrink the machine, but a reactor consumes enormous lengths of tape that industry cannot yet supply cheaply.
robotic servicing exists in research machines; continuous commercial duty cycles have never been demonstrated.
separation is done industrially at small scale, not at the scale a fleet of fusion plants would need.

pathway.milestone: assembly of the ITER experiment in France and compact high-field tokamaks aiming at net gain
pathway.unlocks: real data on burning-plasma behaviour and long-pulse control.

pathway.milestone: pilot plants that deliver electricity to a grid and test breeding blankets
pathway.unlocks: evidence that the fuel cycle can close.

pathway.milestone: a first demonstration power plant with closed tritium breeding and reliable remote maintenance
pathway.unlocks: a design stable enough to be copied rather than reinvented.
fleet-scale baseload power, limited mainly by tritium, lithium-6 and superconducting-tape supply.
